♻ ☆ Quadratic effective energy--momentum tensor on uniform-density hypersurfaces during slow-roll inflation
Inyong Cho
We investigate the quadratic-order effective energy-momentum tensor (2EMT) of scalar cosmological perturbations on uniform-density hypersurfaces during slow-roll inflation. The 2EMT is a gauge-fixed effective source rather than a gauge-invariant observable. We impose the complete scalar gauge conditions $δρ=0$ and $E=0$, express all perturbations in terms of the Bardeen potential $Ψ$, and distinguish the strict infrared and ultraviolet limits from the intermediate regimes. The uniform-density time shift differs from the comoving one by an explicitly gradient-suppressed term, $Q_{\mathrm{UD}}-Q_{\mathrm{C}}=-ΔΨ/[3{\mathcal H}({\mathcal H}'-{\mathcal H}^2)]$. The two sources vanish at zero gradient, while their first nonzero infrared coefficients differ and give $w_{\rm raw}\simeq-1/3$ at leading slow-roll order. In the intermediate infrared, all four gauges have this leading ratio, with gauge-dependent amplitudes. In the ultraviolet, the longitudinal, spatially-flat, and comoving gauges give $w_{\rm raw}\simeq1/3$, whereas the uniform-density gauge gives $w_{\rm raw}\simeq1$. The common $1/ε$ enhancement of the matter-clock gauges reflects the slow evolution of their clocks; the additional uniform-density $1/σ_2^2$ enhancement originates from the Laplacian contribution to the density constraint. Neither enhancement is interpreted as a gauge-independent physical instability, and the gauge reconstruction must remain perturbatively small.

♻ ☆ Stokes Phenomena between AdS/CFT and dS/CFT
Masazumi Honda, Kotaro Shinmyo
As parameters are varied, the set of saddle points contributing to a (path) integral may change discontinuously, leading to a corresponding change in the asymptotic expansion of the integral. This behavior is known as the Stokes phenomenon. We explore this phenomenon in the context of the analytic continuation problem relating the AdS/CFT and dS/CFT correspondences. In this paper, we study these correspondences for three-dimensional pure gravity and two-dimensional Liouville theory, using independent calculations in bulk minisuperspace and in the boundary Liouville zero-mode. In the bulk, the dS contour selects a single saddle and yields the tunneling wave function. Upon continuation to AdS, the contour instead selects an infinite family of saddles. The boundary calculation independently reproduces the same Stokes structure at leading semiclassical order, providing a nontrivial holographic consistency check. Our construction also offers a contour prescription for the conformal factor problem in Euclidean AdS$_3$ quantum gravity within minisuperspace.

♻ ☆ Holographic covering and the fortuity of black holes

We propose a classification of BPS states in holographic CFTs into monotone and fortuitous, based on their behaviors in the large $N$ limit. Intuitively, monotone BPS states form infinite sequences with increasing rank $N$, while fortuitous ones exist within finite ranges of consecutive ranks. A precise definition is formulated using supercharge cohomology. We conjecture that under the AdS/CFT correspondence, monotone BPS states are dual to smooth horizonless geometries, and fortuitous ones are responsible for typical black hole microstates and give dominant contributions to the entropy. We present supporting evidence for our conjectures in the ${\cal N}=4$ SYM and symmetric product orbifolds.

♻ ☆ 0.5 eV QCD Axion Cosmology
Noah Bray-Ali
The best available determination of the present expansion rate of the universe using late-universe observations, by the SH0ES collaboration in 2025, differs by more than seven standard deviations from the value of the Hubble constant determined by the Planck collaboration in 2018 using early-universe observations and the standard cold dark matter cosmology with cosmological constant, a discrepancy known as the Hubble tension. Within a spatially flat, isotropic, and homogeneous expanding-universe solution of the field equations of general relativity with cosmological constant, the SH0ES value for the Hubble constant implies roughly twice as many baryons as the standard cosmology, provided that one retains the Planck values for the energy density of cold dark matter in the present universe and for the cosmological constant. A novel cosmology is proposed --- in terms of cooling dark matter made of quantum chromodynamic (QCD) axions with present number density six times that of the photons in the cosmic microwave background --- which realizes this straightforward, doubled-baryons scenario for resolving the Hubble tension.

♻ ☆ Landau-Ginzburg Theory of a Holographic Superconductor: A Horizon Perspective on the Zero-Temperature Ground State
Sejin Kim, Yunseok Seo
We investigate the effect of a quartic scalar self-interaction, $λ|φ|^4$, on a holographic superconductor in which non-linear electrodynamic couplings generate a superconducting dome containing an extended Lifshitz regime. The quartic interaction leaves the linearized scalar dynamics around the normal phase unchanged while modifying the non-linear solutions where the scalar field is large. As $λ$ increases, the solutions within the dome pass through three stages. The Lifshitz region shrinks until its scaling solution disappears at $λ^*$, leaving a no-AdS region, beyond whose edge the flows end before reaching any asymptotic region, and above $λ_c$ the dome consists entirely of asymptotically AdS hairy black holes. At the bottom of the dome we identify the point where the horizon value of the scalar field is largest, which we refer to as the critical point. There this value lies at the deepest symmetry-breaking minimum that the horizon effective potential, of Landau-Ginzburg form, can have. Unlike a conventional Landau-Ginzburg description, this interpretation rests on the scalar field at the horizon rather than on the boundary order parameter. Below $λ^*$, the constant scalar of the Lifshitz fixed point sits instead at the minimum of the effective potential of its asymptotic scaling region.

♻ ☆ Quantum particle production and radiative properties of a new bumblebee black hole

In this work, we investigate the quantum and radiative properties of a recently proposed static bumblebee black hole arising from a general Lorentz-violating vacuum configuration. The analysis begins with the geometric structure of the solution and the thermodynamic temperature obtained from the surface-gravity prescription. The associated thermodynamic topological structure is also examined. Quantum particle production is then analyzed for bosonic and fermionic fields using the tunneling method. Analytic greybody bounds are derived for spin-0, spin-1, spin-2, and spin-1/2 fields. Furthermore, full greybody factors are computed with the sixth-order WKB method, together with the corresponding absorption cross sections and their characteristic spin-dependent peak patterns. These results support the evaluation of the evaporation lifetimes and the emission rates of energy and particle modes associated with each spin contribution, followed by a comparison of the high-frequency regime with other Lorentz-violating geometries, including the metric bumblebee, metric-affine bumblebee, Kalb-Ramond, and non-commutative Kalb-Ramond black holes. In addition, greybody factors are obtained using a quasinormal-mode-based prescription.

♻ ☆ Information geometry and entanglement under phase-space deformation through nonsymplectic congruence transformation
Shilpa Nandi, Pinaki Patra
We investigate the relationship between Fisher-Rao (FR) information geometry and Gaussian quantum correlations under nonsymplectic phase-space transformations, with particular emphasis on noncommutative (NC) deformation implemented through the Bopp shift. Using the established affine invariance of the FR-metric, we examine the transformation properties of Gaussian covariance matrices and the positive partial transpose (PPT) criterion under invertible congruence transformations. For a bipartite Gaussian system, we demonstrate that keeping the canonical partial-transpose (PT) matrix fixed in the deformed phase space produces deformation-dependent spectral shifts that may cross the conventional PPT threshold. When the PT operation is transported together with the covariance and commutation matrices, the physical PPT spectrum and separability classification remain invariant under local Darboux transformations. We further investigate a two-dimensional anisotropic oscillator in NC phase space, where the deformation parameters modify the effective canonical Hamiltonian and consequently influence the Gaussian ground-state correlations and entanglement between canonical modes. The corresponding FR-geometry reveals that the original covariance manifold possesses constant negative scalar curvature. In contrast, the pure symmetric normal-form covariance family is intrinsically one-dimensional and flat. These results distinguish the statistical geometry of Gaussian covariance matrices from the physical quantum correlations determined by the Hamiltonian, commutation structure, and subsystem decomposition.
♻ ☆ Resonant electroweak clouds around Schwarzschild black holes
Carlos Herdeiro, Eugen Radu
We construct nonlinear electroweak clouds around Schwarzschild black holes in the bosonic Weinberg-Salam theory. These configurations are supported by harmonically time-dependent charged gauge fields, while their energy-momentum tensor remains static. Regularity at the horizon imposes a resonance condition relating the field frequency to the horizon electrostatic potential. Unlike linear clouds, these solutions exhibit a finite mass and electric charge gap, and exist only up to a maximal horizon size. We obtain both magnetic and electric clouds, including spherically symmetric and dipolar configurations, which reduce to electroweak balls in the vanishing-horizon limit. We also report a new family of dipolar electroweak balls, which can be energetically favoured over their spherical and magnetic counterparts at fixed electric charge. Our results, obtained in the probe limit for electroweak couplings away from their measured values, establish a new realization of nonlinear resonant vector hair in a non-Abelian gauge-Higgs theory.

♻ ☆ Flat Space Physics from AdS Actions
Walker Melton
Flat spacetimes are foliated by hyperbolic slices that are geometrically three-dimensional de Sitter or anti-de Sitter spaces. As such, it is possible to construct flat space holographic dualities by applying the AdS/CFT bulk-to-boundary dictionary slice by slice. In this work, we reduce 4D actions for massless scalars in both Minkowski space and Klein space and massive scalars in Minkowski space to actions on these 3D dS and AdS slices. In both Minkowski and Klein space, the reduced theories have a continuous spectrum of fields originating from the reduction over the noncompact $x^2$ direction. These actions are linked by boundary terms arising from field configurations discontinuous across the lightcone. In the massless case, different asymptotic limits of the reduced field near the boundary of the unit hyperbolic slice replicate either lightcone or null infinity limits of the field; in the massive case, only one boundary mode of the reduced field has a simple geometric interpretation.

♻ ☆ Searching for cosmic strings via black hole spin-down
Sameer Ahmed, Michael J. Kavic, Steven L. Liebling, Matthew Lippert, Mohammad Mian, John Simonetti
Cosmic strings that are attached to rapidly spinning black holes can extract significant amounts of rotational energy and angular momentum. Here, we study the effect on primordial black holes, which are expected to form with one or more cosmic strings attached. Although large primordial black holes of mass greater than O$(10 M_\odot)$ are predicted to rapidly spin up due to accretion soon after forming, we argue that cosmic strings will spin them down again. We show that if there are cosmic strings with tension greater than $10^{-20}$, and, provided at least one remains attached, the spins of large primordial black holes should consequently be observed to be near zero. We also investigate the effect on a supermassive black hole of capturing a cosmic string and discuss the possibility of observing the subsequent spin down by its effect on a pulsar orbiting the black hole.

♻ ☆ Stochastic gravitational waves from narrow-band cosmological magnetic fields

We calculate the spectrum of gravitational waves generated by a cosmological magnetic field with a narrow-band power spectrum. For a magnetic spectrum narrowly peaked at a comoving wavenumber $k_c$, we find that the gravitational wave signal has a maximum at $2k_c$ and, as expected from momentum conservation, has a sharp cutoff at that scale. We apply this analysis to an ultralight dark matter model of magnetogenesis operating around recombination, in which an axion-photon coupling generates a helical magnetic field by parametric resonance. We determine the conditions for the resulting gravitational waves to enter the frequency range of pulsar timing experiments. Although the required frequency can be reached for sufficiently large coupling, the corresponding amplitude is below the experimental sensitivity for physically allowed energy densities of the magnetic field. We generalize this conclusion to models of magnetogenesis operating at other epochs, estimating as $T \simeq 160$ MeV the temperature of a magnetogenesis process assumed to be the source of the stochastic gravitational wave background suggested by pulsar timing arrays. We place the lower bound $T \gtrsim 1$-10 MeV on such viable models.

☆ Dynamics of a Single-Domain Dissipative Magnetic Gyroscope in Electric and Magnetic Fields
Y. B. Band, Igor Kuzmenko
We formulate the coupled spin--rotation dynamics of a single-domain symmetric top ferromagnetic needle (a magnetic gyroscope) in static magnetic and electric fields. The conservative Hamiltonian contains the rotational kinetic energy, the magnetocrystalline and shape anisotropy, the Zeeman energy, the electrostatic energy of the dipole induced in the conducting needle, the linear magnetoelectric coupling, and the relativistic motional (spin-orbit) coupling. Gilbert damping is introduced, and in an electric field, Debye relaxation of the induced electric dipole of the conducting needle also results in dissipation. We give the equations of motion in the laboratory and body-fixed frames, with singularity-free quaternion kinematics. For a 120-nm-long single-domain cobalt needle in a 0.5~T field we find: (i) because the anisotropy field ($\approx 1.3$~T) exceeds the applied magnetic field, the spin reverses direction several times during the initial Gilbert-damping transient, and the parity of the number of reversals determines whether the easy axis ends up parallel or antiparallel to the spin; (ii) after the transient the needle librates about the field---precession accompanied by nutation at twice the precession frequency---with a period of about 20~ns, consistent with the libration period $2π(I_1/μB)^{1/2}$, while the Zeeman and rotational kinetic energies oscillate out of phase and the total energy is conserved; (iii) a static electric field $\mathbf E$ exerts on the conducting needle a shape-dependent polarization torque that tends to align the long axis of the needle with $\mathbf E$. The torques due to the magnetoelectric interaction and motional magnetic fields ($\lesssim1~μ$T) are negligible compared with the polarization torque. A conducting needle can therefore serve as a magnetometer only if $E\ll E_c$.

Indentation is widely used to infer the mechanical state of biological materials like the actomyosin cortex. It reduces a single force-indentation curve to an apparent modulus. The cortex, however, is a pre-tensioned, heterogeneous fibre network. We show that this inference is ambiguous. The same amount of weakening can leave the indentation force unchanged or lower it tenfold, depending on where it lies relative to the probe. The force reflects how the probe couples to the tensioned, load-bearing structure, not the amount of weakening. We combine molecular dynamics simulations of a pressure-loaded, crosslinked fibre network indented by a rigid sphere with a continuum membrane solution. We represent the simulated force-depth response by a two-term fit, $F\propto aδ+bδ^{3/2}$, with $a$ reflecting the global tension, and $b$ the stiffening with depth. At a fixed fraction of weakened bonds, diffuse weakening lowers the force by a factor of about 1.5. A weak cluster beneath the probe lowers it 8-12-fold, because the slack cluster decouples the probe from the tension. When the clusters are displaced from the contact, the force returns to within 15% of the healthy value. Two opposite effects cancel. The clusters soften the whole layer, which lowers its tension and the force. But they also channel the load through the intact network beneath the probe, which stiffens it locally and raises the force. The shape of the curve retains what the force level hides. The coefficient $a$ reflects the softened layer when clusters beside the probe keep the force near the healthy value. The local exponent $α=\mathrm{d}\ln F/\mathrm{d}\lnδ$ increases with depth in every configuration except when a cluster lies beneath the probe, where the two-term form no longer applies. Detecting localised weakening requires spatial sampling and analysis of the curve shape, not a single fitted modulus.

The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. A notable example is a few-layer NiI2 multiferroic, which exhibits coexisting chiral spin textures and (anti)ferroelectricity, accompanied by strong magnetoelectric coupling; by simultaneously breaking time-reversal and spatial-inversion symmetry, NiI2 shows new physical properties such as unique mutual control of chiral magnetism and polarization with giant magnetoelectric coupling, ultrafast electromagnon excitations and odd-parity p-wave magnetism. We emphasize the importance of magneto-opto-electric cross-correlative measurements in establishing intrinsic multiferroic behaviour and outline future research directions for both fundamental studies and device applications.

comment: Defect-trapped hydrogen (DTH) has been experimentally demonstrated to reconstruct screw dislocation core and to enable normal stress coupling. The resulted atomic decohesion will allow the formation of H2 molecule releasing chemical energy and driving rapid crack growth. Main text 13 Pages, 1 table plus 4 figures

In the ideal noiseless simulation setting, we see that the survival probability of the ground and the excited states within the target $CAS$ subspace is unity, because the total photon number and the photon number in the two spin sectors $α$ and $β$ are preserved. Charge density waves are among the earliest known ordered states in quantum materials, yet they have re-emerged at the center of modern discussions of topology, symmetry breaking, and collective dynamics. In several material classes, charge-density-wave order reshapes electronic bands, boundary states, defect structures, and electromagnetic responses in ways that invite a topological interpretation. Real-space imaging has shown that incommensurate order can form networks of phase defects rather than uniform modulations. Boundary-resolved spectroscopy has revealed in-gap modes whose existence and spatial structure track the charge-density-wave order, although such observations remain confined to a single material family. In Weyl materials, density-wave gaps have been linked to axion-like magnetoelectric response, placing the charge-density-wave phase within a dynamical-field description of the effective action. In kagome metals, charge order is intertwined with Berry curvature, unconventional symmetry breaking, and superconductivity. These developments have led to the term "topological charge density wave," but the phrase describes several physically distinct phenomena. We distinguish three meanings: (i) topology of the order parameter and its defects, (ii) topology of the charge-density-wave-reconstructed electronic structure and its boundary modes, and (iii) axion-like electromagnetic response generated by density-wave order. The experimental and theoretical support for these three meanings differs substantially. This Perspective traces the development of these ideas, clarifies the evidence behind each class, identifies unresolved questions and points of debate, and outlines experimental criteria for establishing topology in charge-density-wave states.

Second, the competition is controlled by the detuning from the VHS. While CDW dominates near the VHS filling and at higher temperatures, PDW becomes the leading instability on either side of the VHS and at lower temperatures. This mechanism naturally produces two superconducting regions separated by a CDW-dominated regime, providing a possible qualitative explanation for the experimentally observed separation between SC1 and SC2.

While in one dimension an area law for the Renyi-0 entropy guarantees an exact matrix product state representation with a bond dimension independent of the system size, an analogous statement does not hold for general states in two dimensions (2D). In this work, we focus on two families of 2D translation-invariant Gaussian fermionic states: single-band BCS superconductors and half-filled two-band insulators (including semimetals). We also establish equivalent characterizations in terms of compactly supported Wannier-type orbitals and the momentum-space wavefunction, relating the spatial extent of these orbitals and the structure of the wavefunction to the required bond dimension.

Specifically, we consider two examples of observables which give large signals despite the randomness of the dynamics: first order out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) in unstructured random circuits without conservation laws and time-ordered charge-charge correlators (TOCs) in particle number-preserving random circuits. We design and implement algorithms that combine Monte Carlo sampling and tensor network methods to approximate the series. We observe numerically that the computational complexity of approximating TOCs and OTOCs scales polynomially in the circuit size and in the target precision. We study the accuracy of these algorithms by directly mapping their ensemble-averaged errors to partition functions of replica statistical models, allowing for perturbative analysis and numerics in $1$d brickwork geometries. Our theoretical analysis explains the empirical observation of polynomial complexity of these algorithms and is consistent with polynomial complexity extending to arbitrarily small precision and to the thermodynamic limit.

We study magnetic skyrmions in a two-dimensional quasicrystalline lattice using a classical Heisenberg model with Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interactions and an external magnetic field. The competition between the skyrmion--skyrmion repulsion and an emergent quasiperiodic pinning landscape gives rise to a sequence of distinct skyrmion lattice configurations as a function of field. The resulting hierarchy of quasiperiodic pinning potentials, characterized by closely spaced quasi-degenerate minima, enables a quasi-continuous suppression of the skyrmion density as the saturation field is approached, in sharp contrast to the strongly first-order collapse of skyrmion crystals on periodic lattices. This provides a direct mechanism for controlling the topological charge and, consequently, the emergent gauge field for itinerant electrons. As a consequence, the Hall conductivity can be strongly modified with small changes in the magnetic field and driven smoothly to zero near saturation. This field-controlled tunability, rooted in the underlying multistability, identifies quasicrystalline magnets as a platform for tunable topological textures, with potential applications in magnetic memory and magnetoelectronic response.

We introduce the parafermionic truncated Wigner approximation ($p$TWA), a semiclassical phase-space method for studying the nonequilibrium dynamics of multilevel quantum systems, including $\mathbb{Z}_n$ Fock parafermions. Motivated by the fractional exchange statistics of Fock parafermions, we express the Hamiltonian in a basis of local Hubbard operators that closes under commutation. This representation yields a Lie--Poisson formulation in which stochastic sampling of the initial state is followed by deterministic semiclassical evolution. We benchmark the method for single-site clock dynamics, a fully connected $\mathbb{Z}_n$ clock model that generalizes the Lipkin--Meshkov--Glick model, long-range $\mathbb{Z}_3$ clock chains, and clean and disordered one-dimensional Fock parafermion chains. The method captures qualitative features of the quantum benchmarks, including excitation spreading, disorder-induced suppression of transport, and long-time imbalance plateaus. In the single-hopping parafermion chains, it predicts slower domain-wall relaxation than time-evolving block decimation.

♻ ☆ Landau Theory of Black Brane Phase Transitions from Kasner Singularities

We develop a Landau theory of a continuous black-brane phase transition using the geometry of the black-hole interior. The normal phase has a Reissner--Nordström Cauchy horizon, whereas the scalarized phase ends at a Kasner singularity. A conserved radial charge determines the grand potential from either endpoint and permits a direct phase comparison. At the critical point, we show analytically that the quadratic correction to the conserved radial charge vanishes. Using the inverse Kasner scalar velocity as an interior order parameter, we then construct a Landau potential whose coefficients are determined entirely from the terminal singularity. The Iyer--Wald first law relates this potential to the conventional boundary Landau theory and fixes its quartic coefficient. For two models with different scalar self-interactions, the resulting theory predicts the critical scaling of the Kasner order parameter and the grand-potential difference between the phases, in agreement with fully backreacted numerical solutions.

The numerical renormalization group (NRG) approach was developed to identify and quantify different equilibrium regimes of quantum impurity systems (QISs) with unprecedented accuracy by a tailored finite size representation. Out of equilibrium, the steady-state density operator is not of the Boltzmannian form but one that is determined by the imposed boundary conditions. We extend the NRG to the nonequilibrium setting by augmenting each Wilson site with a reservoir, whose coupling functions are calculated via a continuous fraction expansion in order to recover the continuum limit exactly. The nonequilibrium parameters such as a finite bias as well as a finite temperature gradient enters through the Bloch-Redfield tensor (BRT), whose zero eigenvector gives the steady-state density operator. We used the resulting open chain full density matrix (OC-FDM) approach with an effective single lead description to investigate the charge and spin transport through a quantum dot (QD) under finite bias and temperature gradient. The influence of lead asymmetry and an external magnetic field on the transport properties are also studied. For completeness, we have also investigated local properties of the QD, such as charge fluctuations and find excellent agreement with real-time quantum Monte Carlo (RT-QMC) data. The OC-FDM approach was able to explore Kondo energy scales as low as $T_K/D \approx 10^{-8}$ in the non-equilibrium regime, as well as show convergence with the established equilibrium benchmarks, such as a quantitative agreement with full density matrix numerical renormalization group (FDM-NRG) and Fermi-liquid scaling at small bias and temperature. Owing to the effective single lead description, a single OC-FDM data point takes orders of magnitude less time on a standard laptop, compared to other state-of-the-art numerical methods.

♻ ☆ Fractional quantization in gapless flat bands with ill-defined topology and divergent quantum geometry

Fractional quantum anomalous Hall (FQAH) effect, a zero-magnetic-field lattice analog of the fractional quantum Hall effect, offers a unique pathway toward fault-tolerant quantum computation and deep insights into the interplay of topology and strong correlations. The exploration has been successfully guided by the paradigm of ideal flat Chern bands, which mimic Landau levels in both band topology and local quantum geometry. Yet, given the boundless potential for Bloch bands in lattice systems, it remains a significant open question whether FQAH states can arise in scenarios fundamentally distinct from this paradigm. Here we turn to a class of gapless flat bands, featuring (i) ill-defined band topology, (ii) non-quantized Berry flux, (iii) divergent quantum geometry at singular band touchings, (iv) highly fluctuating and far-from-ideal quantum geometry across the Brillouin zone. Our exact diagonalization and density matrix renormalization group calculations unambiguously demonstrate an FQAH phase that is virtually independent of the interaction strength, persisting from the weak-interaction to the strong-interaction limit. We find the stability of the FQAH states does not uniquely correlate with the singularity strength. Instead, the many-body topological order can adapt to the singular and fluctuating quantum geometric landscape by spontaneously developing an inhomogeneous carrier distribution, while its quenching is accompanied by a drop in the occupation-weighted Berry flux. Our work reveals a profound interplay between local quantum geometry and many-body correlation, and significantly expands the exploration space for the FQAH effect and correlated phenomena in general.

The logic applies to regions with sharp corners, from which we derive several universal properties regarding corner entanglement. These universal properties follow from a set of locally-checkable conditions on the wavefunction. We also define a quantity $(\mathfrak{c}_{\text{tot}})_{\text{min}}$ that reflects the robustness of corner entanglement contributions, and show that it provides an obstruction to a gapped boundary. One reward from our analysis is that we can construct a local gapped Hamiltonian within the same chiral gapped phase from a given wavefunction; we conjecture that it is closer to the low-energy renormalization group fixed point than the original parent Hamiltonian. Our analysis of corner entanglement reveals the emergence of a universal conformal geometry encoded in the entanglement structure of bulk regions of chiral gapped states that is not visible in topological field theory. Our formalism also gives an explanation of the modular commutator formula for the chiral central charge.

♻ ☆ Interference-caged quantum many-body scars: Local ETH-violation witnesses and deformation stability
Tao-Lin Tan, Yi-Ping Huang
Many-body interference can render an exact eigenstate locally nonthermal by canceling a microscopic process active in thermal states. We formulate the Fock-space analogue of compact flat-band localization as \emph{interference caging}: escape amplitudes cancel exactly across the active boundary of a set of product configurations. We give sufficient conditions to reduce this configuration-dependent cancellation to a fixed real-space region, yielding a bounded local caging operator. Its positive square vanishes on the caged eigenstate and witnesses violation of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH) if its microcanonical expectation for the same Hamiltonian and energy density remains bounded away from zero in the thermodynamic limit. We call these states \emph{interference-caged quantum many-body scars} (ICQMBS) when they form a vanishing fraction of a symmetry-resolved bulk energy window whose typical eigenstates are locally thermal for every bounded local observable. The mechanism is independent of quasiparticle, algebraic, or symmetry-based constructions and compatible with Hilbert-space fragmentation. Our chiral-shell search constructs exact caged eigenstates from allowed transitions without a preselected wavefunction, target subspace, or ladder operator. We identify local ETH-violation witnesses, test their deformation stability, and demonstrate thermal contrast in two systems. In the spin-1 XY chain, we recover the known scar tower, also describable through quasiparticles and projector embedding, and prove ICQMBS throughout an open interval of compatible exchange couplings in the thermodynamic limit. In the square-lattice quantum dimer model, we construct exact caged eigenstates and local operators from plaquette flips on fixed-width strips under a checkerboard phase deformation; finite-size microcanonical comparisons support thermal contrast.

♻ ☆ Associator Defects in Non-Unitary String-Nets

We study obstructions to realizing fusion categories in physical Hilbert spaces by varying positive inner products on elementary fusion spaces. We introduce an associator defect to measure the smallest failure of recoupling maps to preserve the induced inner products in order to do so. By using a determinant identity from the pentagon equation, we prove that the minimum is attained and vanishes when the category is unitarizable. As an example, we compute the defect for the Yang-Lee category and its double, studying its behavior under stacking and passage to Drinfeld centers, which results in a Morita-invariant measure of bulk nonunitarity. We also obtain lower bounds for quantum-group categories with fusion multiplicities. Finally, we study how these obstructions appear in physical realizations of fusion. Under the stated assumptions on local splitting operations and coherent measurements, a positive defect imposes quantitative tradeoffs between implementation errors and operator norms. We also obtain bounds on the response to local perturbations. These results show how the failure of categorical unitarity will place quantitative constraints on physical realizations of potential fusion.

♻ ☆ A Correlated Route to Antiferromagnetic Spintronics
Joel Bobadilla, Alberto Camjayi
Antiferromagnets are attractive for spintronics owing to their vanishing net magnetization and ultrafast spin dynamics, yet their spin-compensated electronic structure has long confined them to passive roles. Here we identify a symmetry selection rule that overcomes this limitation: in a collinear antiferromagnet, a spin-polarized dc charge current requires the simultaneous breaking of particle--hole symmetry and of the equivalence between the two magnetic sublattices, either one alone leaving the polarization identically zero. We demonstrate the rule in the doped antiferromagnetic Hubbard model within dynamical mean-field theory: doping and a uniform magnetic field each break one of the two symmetries, and electronic correlations convert the resulting asymmetries into a sizable, field-tunable polarization of the charge current. The polarization is largest deep in the ordered phase and reverses sign at an emergent compensation point, set by the hierarchy of spin-dependent scattering rates and not dictated by symmetry, at which the dominant conducting spin species is interchanged. In correlated altermagnetic Hubbard models, the same two symmetries are broken structurally, by the sublattice-alternating hopping pattern: the field-driven mechanism identified here and the altermagnetic one are two realizations of a single selection rule. Electronic correlations thus emerge as an active ingredient for spintronics in structurally conventional collinear antiferromagnets.

BaCo2(AsO4)2 (BCAO) is an insulating Kitaev quantum spin liquid candidate with a rich low-temperature phase diagram. Below 5 K, it exhibits double-zigzag magnetic order. Upon application of an in-plane magnetic field, the magnetic structure first transforms into an up-up-down (UUD) state near 0.12 T and then enters a fully spin-polarized ferromagnetic (FM) state near 0.5 T. In the narrow field regime close to the polarized phase, a finite residual thermal conductivity has been reported, suggesting a possible field-induced quantum spin liquid phase. Using neutron scattering, we show that the field-induced double-zigzag-to-UUD transition near 0.15 T is accompanied by the emergence of a cluster of localized UUD spin excitations that coexist with conventional spin waves. Upon further increasing field, BCAO undergoes a first-order UUD-to-FM transition with coexistence of UUD and FM phases, accompanied by a sharp response in the spin Seebeck coefficient. These results do not support a quantum spin liquid scenario near the UUD-to-FM critical field. Instead, modeling indicates that the broad excitations arise from bound spin-flip pairs, while a low-lying dispersive branch near the FM phase boundary carries the same sign of magnetization as the FM order. These excitations naturally account for the observed sign of the spin Seebeck response and are likely relevant to the thermal conductivity near the critical field.

♻ ☆ 0.5 eV QCD Axion Cosmology

The best available determination of the present expansion rate of the universe using late-universe observations, by the SH0ES collaboration in 2025, differs by more than seven standard deviations from the value of the Hubble constant determined by the Planck collaboration in 2018 using early-universe observations and the standard cold dark matter cosmology with cosmological constant, a discrepancy known as the Hubble tension. Within a spatially flat, isotropic, and homogeneous expanding-universe solution of the field equations of general relativity with cosmological constant, the SH0ES value for the Hubble constant implies roughly twice as many baryons as the standard cosmology, provided that one retains the Planck values for the energy density of cold dark matter in the present universe and for the cosmological constant. A novel cosmology is proposed --- in terms of cooling dark matter made of quantum chromodynamic (QCD) axions with present number density six times that of the photons in the cosmic microwave background --- which realizes this straightforward, doubled-baryons scenario for resolving the Hubble tension.

♻ ☆ Colloquium: Semi-Dirac Fermions in Quantum Matter

This article reviews the recent progress on the subject of semi-Dirac fermions, two dimensional quasiparticles that disperse quadratically, as Galilean invariant particles, or linearly, as massless relativistic particles, depending on their direction of motion. These quasiparticles exist at phase boundaries set by the continuous change in the connectivity of Fermi surfaces, known as Lifshitz transitions. The basic properties and the current experimental evidence of the existence of these quasiparticles in both synthetic lattices and quantum materials are presented. The many-body problem of semi-Dirac fermions is discussed from a theoretical perspective with an eye to physical observables of relevance to experiments.

♻ ☆ A Perspective on Topological Charge Density Wave Materials
Chun-Tung Lien, Nidhish Thiruthukkal Puthenveettil, Alexander A. Balandin, Md Shafayat Hossain
Charge density waves are among the earliest known ordered states in quantum materials, yet they have re-emerged at the center of modern discussions of topology, symmetry breaking, and collective dynamics. In several material classes, charge-density-wave order reshapes electronic bands, boundary states, defect structures, and electromagnetic responses in ways that invite a topological interpretation. Real-space imaging has shown that incommensurate order can form networks of phase defects rather than uniform modulations. Boundary-resolved spectroscopy has revealed in-gap modes whose existence and spatial structure track the charge-density-wave order, although such observations remain confined to a single material family. In Weyl materials, density-wave gaps have been linked to axion-like magnetoelectric response, placing the charge-density-wave phase within a dynamical-field description of the effective action. In kagome metals, charge order is intertwined with Berry curvature, unconventional symmetry breaking, and superconductivity. These developments have led to the term "topological charge density wave," but the phrase describes several physically distinct phenomena. We distinguish three meanings: (i) topology of the order parameter and its defects, (ii) topology of the charge-density-wave-reconstructed electronic structure and its boundary modes, and (iii) axion-like electromagnetic response generated by density-wave order. The experimental and theoretical support for these three meanings differs substantially. This Perspective traces the development of these ideas, clarifies the evidence behind each class, identifies unresolved questions and points of debate, and outlines experimental criteria for establishing topology in charge-density-wave states.

☆ Open Heavy Flavor in Nuclear Collisions: From Lattice QCD to Observables
Yu Fu, Steffen A. Bass, Tharun Krishna, Ralf Rapp, Weiyao Ke
Heavy quarks serve as excellent probes of the Quark-Gluon-Plasma (QGP) produced in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions. Here, we report on a comprehensive framework that transports charm quarks from their initial production through the QGP medium, hadronization, and the hadronic phase to final observables in experiments. For the transport through the QGP fireball, which is described by 2+1D relativistic viscous fluid dynamics, we employ an extended Langevin equation that combines elastic diffusion processes with medium-induced radiation, including interference effects. The charm-quark transport coefficients are derived from nonperturbative $T$-matrix interactions, which are constrained by lattice QCD and also produce an equation of state for the thermal medium which is consistent with the one employed in the hydrodynamic simulations. Pre-hadronic resonant states which emerge in the $T$-matrix near the QGP transition temperature naturally lead to a transition to hadronic degrees of freedom. This transition is realized in two different approaches: a coalescence model augmented with 4-momentum conservation and the resonance recombination model, both supplemented with fragmentation functions constrained by charm-hadron spectra in proton-proton collisions at the LHC and RHIC. The late-stage rescattering of charm hadrons is assessed with schematic heavy-light cross sections implemented into a hadronic transport model. We report results for the nuclear modification factors and elliptic flows of $D^0$ and $D_s^+$ mesons and $Λ_c^+$ baryons, together with the $D_s^+/D^0$ and $Λ_c^+/D^0$ yield ratios. The calculations are compared with measurements from the ALICE and CMS collaborations in Pb--Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\NN}}=5$\,TeV and with STAR data in Au-Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\NN}}=200$\,GeV.

The motivation is twofold: the $σ$-meson is the lightest scalar resonance in QCD and is therefore the natural extensions to the pions of the classical Skyrme model, while its interpretation as a pseudo-Goldstone boson of spontaneously broken scale symmetry is supported by recent studies of gravitational form factors and related developments. Although the $σ$-meson is a broad resonance, for static observables it can be treated as real particle since its line-shape is not expected to be essential. A combined fit to static nucleon observables yields $χ^2/\mathrm{dof} $ close to unity, with substantial improvement over the original Skyrme model, while simultaneously reproducing the physical value of $F_π$, the overall scale of the model.

Within the DGLV framework, we calculate the radiation spectrum at first order in opacity and to first-subeikonal accuracy, retaining finite heavy-quark and effective gluon masses. Subleading corrections to the longitudinal propagator poles generate mass-dependent modifications of both the residue denominators and formation phases. For rotationally symmetric transverse-momentum integration domains, all contributions linear in the transverse flow velocity vanish after full azimuthal integration, while a nonzero static first-subeikonal correction remains. For representative medium parameters, this correction increases the integrated fractional radiative energy loss by approximately $10$--$20\%$, depending on the quark mass, initial energy, and path length. At the differential level, transverse flow produces a dipolar angular anisotropy, enhancing radiation along the flow direction and suppressing it in the opposite direction.

A microscopic approach to optical potential calculations, based on the leading term in the spectator expansion of the optical potential operator and carried out in momentum space, has been successful in describing nucleon elastic scattering above 100 MeV. However, high computational cost precludes the inclusion of all physics relevant to scattering, such as the tensor part of the nucleon-nucleon (NN) amplitude, three-nucleon forces, multiple scattering and medium effects. Also, this approach does not provide any nucleon-nucleus scattering wave functions needed for reaction calculations. In this Letter, we develop a harmonic oscillator expansion version of this approach, which provides the same representation of optical potential both in momentum and coordinate spaces, accelerates calculations by two orders of magnitude, includes the missing tensor component of the NN scattering amplitude and is applicable to nuclei with any spin. We demonstrate convergence of this expansion and clarify the role of the tensor force, which manifests itself mainly in coupling between channels with different spin. Comparison to experimental data is presented for selected cases. The methodology could be extended for scattering of other projectiles (hadronic and pionic), small complex nuclei and hypernuclei. It also suggests a pathway for including more complicated physics into the scheme and extending it to lower energies. It could be also helpful in assessing the accuracy of upcoming scattering emulators.

Heating at the reference quadrupole constraint yields compensating thermal and quasiparticle-energy factors, so similar gap reductions produce nearly common attenuation. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

We describe our method, which can be readily applied to similar processes. We observe rapid convergence within the validity range of the forward expansion. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entire phase space can be covered when this approach is combined with the high-energy expansion.

☆ Mapping the multimessenger horizon for $γ$-ray counterparts of cosmic neutrinos
Tianyi Ding, Jose Alonso Carpio, Ali Kheirandish, Kohta Murase
The joint detection of high-energy neutrinos and $γ$-rays offers a powerful probe of the most energetic astrophysical accelerators, linking hadronic interactions to observable signatures across cosmic distances. Understanding the conditions under which these two messengers can be simultaneously observed is essential for identifying and characterizing the sources of cosmic neutrinos. In this work, we examine the detectability of $γ$-ray cascades associated with neutrino production in source environments that are gamma-ray transparent, focusing on how electromagnetic cascades evolve as $γ$-rays propagate through intergalactic space. By modeling photon interactions with the extragalactic background light and deflections in intergalactic magnetic fields, we determine the minimum neutrino fluence for transient emission and neutrino flux for steady emission required to produce a $γ$-ray counterpart detectable by $γ$-ray observatories, such as Fermi-LAT, HAWC, or LHAASO. This defines a ``multimessenger horizon" -- the region in flux-distance parameter space where neutrinos and $γ$-rays are jointly observable. We consider both energy-binned injection tied to IceCube's sensitivity and a continuous power-law spectrum extending from TeV to PeV energies. Our results reveal that detectability depends strongly on redshift, magnetic field strength, and photon energy, with higher-energy cascades suffering greater attenuation inside filamentary structures. The framework provides new constraints on source opacity, baryon loading, and neutrino production mechanisms, offering a predictive tool for interpreting current events and guiding future multimessenger campaigns.

Their stability follows from an exact accidental parity of the strong sector. Annihilation channels from composite interactions link the thermal relic mass to the strong coupling, allowing masses well beyond the pure electroweak prediction. In the pure electroweak regime, the pair consists of the neutral components of a complex Higgsino-like doublet. Its unsuppressed inelastic $Z$ coupling requires Dark Matter masses above 20 TeV. In the pure strong regime, the suppressed $Z$ coupling of neutral states with vanishing hypercharge arises from strong interactions alone, allowing for smaller splittings and TeV-scale masses. In the third regime, which interpolates between the previous two, the neutral components of multiplets with different hypercharge are mixed. This enhances their inelastic coupling, accommodating the LZ event for masses of a few TeV and splittings around 300 keV, with mixing angles of order $10^\circ$. All three cases provide a thermal Dark Matter candidate able to explain the LZ event, consistently with the solar-capture bounds, the LZ high-energy sideband, and gamma-ray indirect searches.

☆ Plugging the Pion Chimney

Heavy QCD axions and other gluon-coupled axion-like particles (ALPs) with masses from MeV to GeV are well motivated and have been searched for extensively. However, a window around the neutral pion mass, the so-called pion chimney, has escaped every search. There the ALP mixes strongly with the $π^0$ and therefore shares its experimental signatures. We show that the chimney can be closed with existing LHC data. The key point is that mixing changes the lifetimes of the two mass eigenstates but does not make them equal, and at LHC energies the states are boosted enough for the lifetime to decide whether they escape the detector or decay inside it. The ATLAS monojet search constrains the first case and the ATLAS inclusive photon measurement the second, and together they exclude the chimney up to the cutoff of the ALP effective theory. Above the cutoff, LHC searches for the colored states of the simplest ultraviolet completions exclude the rest. We also show that the bound from the $K^+$ width does not reach the chimney, because an ALP passes the same selection as a $π^0$, and we derive an independent, purely kinematic constraint from the measured $π^\pm$-$π^0$ mass splitting.

Boosted dark matter (BDM) realizes this possibility through a two-component scenario in which the annihilation of the heavier component converts part of the mass difference into kinetic energy of the lighter component. We calculate the global 21 cm brightness temperature and its power spectrum in BDM cosmology. The reduced abundance of low-mass halos delays the global absorption feature and shifts the characteristic redshift evolution of the power spectrum. We assess the projected sensitivity of SKA1-Low to these signatures. The sensitivity is strongest at intermediate light-component fractions, where both components remain sufficiently abundant for self-heating to affect structure formation. For $σ_{\rm self1}/m_1\simeq0.1\,{\rm cm^2\,g^{-1}}$, models with $0.2\lesssim r_1\lesssim0.7$ can be distinguished from the fiducial $Λ$CDM prediction at the $95\%$ confidence level under the optimistic forecast. This comparison highlights the unique and complementary role of high-redshift surveys in testing BDM models.

☆ The SymTFT and Quantum Phases of Matter
Salvatore D. Pace, Sakura Schafer-Nameki, Carolyn Zhang
The symmetry topological field theory (SymTFT) provides a unified framework for ordinary and generalized symmetries of quantum many-body systems. By encoding symmetry in a topological theory in one higher dimension, it separates symmetry data from the details of a specific quantum system. In this review, we give a pedagogical introduction to this framework and survey its applications to phases of quantum matter. For fusion category symmetries in ${(1+1)}$d, we explain how the SymTFT characterizes anomalies, classifies gapped phases, and organizes the symmetry structure of gapless phases. We also give a broad overview of further developments of this framework, including extensions to symmetries in higher dimensions, continuous symmetries, fermionic systems, mixed states, and spacetime symmetries.

The BBH hypothesis is individually favored, with $\log_{10}\mathcal{B}_{\rm BBH/TDM}=12.2$ and $11.3$ for GW231123 and GW190521, respectively. However, these values are lower than those typically recovered from matched maximum a posteriori BBH waveforms injected into nearby noise segments. We further perform, for the first time, a joint fit in which domain wall signals from a single underlying scalar field are constrained simultaneously by both events. Although not favored over BBH signals, we find the two events are consistent with a common scalar field, with shared TDM parameters agreeing across independent noise realizations and sky locations. We further find that injected TDM transients are systematically recovered under the BBH hypothesis with large spin parameters, revealing a morphological degeneracy that could mask genuine domain wall signals. This analysis demonstrates that multi-event parameter consistency tests provide a new discriminant for domain wall dark matter searches in upcoming observing runs.

♻ ☆ Searching for New Physics with Reinforcement Learning
Jacky Kumar, Marianne Bouchard, David London
Finding new physics (NP) is the fundamental problem in particle physics today. Studying anomalies, i.e., measurements of low-energy observables whose values disagree with the predictions of the Standard Model (SM), is a powerful search strategy. The SM Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general model-independent framework for parametrizing NP; given some anomalies, it is natural to try to find the SMEFT operator(s) that can explain them. This is a challenging task because (i) the number of SMEFT operators is enormous, and (ii) at loop level there are very complicated correlations among the operators. Analyses by humans typically rely on phenomenological intuition to decide which operators are relevant. This is often biased and does not explore the complete SMEFT operator space. Interestingly, reinforcement learning (RL) techniques excel at tasks that require decision making to achieve their goals. In this paper, we introduce an RL method that can be used to find the SMEFT operators that explain any anomalies. Using some explicit examples, we demonstrate that our RL method can be used to efficiently search for NP at the level of SMEFT. The RL training can be performed efficiently using standard CPU resources, without requiring specialized computing hardware.

The leading $\sim72$ GeV triad coincides with the mass implied by interpreting the reported $\sim43.2$ GeV $γ$-ray line in three nearby clusters as its $γZ$ channel. At this externally fixed mass, the triad reaches $3.0σ$ alone, and $5.1σ$ when combined with the reported line ($3.8σ$ under alternative assumptions; similar values for the nonad). This triad, absent from the ambient (X-ray-uncorrelated) spectrum, presents in different Galactic sectors, strengthens under cosmological (positive) but not negative redshift broadening $Δz$, and peaks at $Δz\simeq 0.05$, consistent with galaxy clusters; its two non-$43$ GeV channels reach $2.4σ$ by themselves. The unified description of these processes clearly confirms the universality of genuine twist-three PDFs and the validity of QCD factorization theorems at this subleading level. The extraction is accompanied by several validation tests, tests of sum rules, comparisons with earlier literature, computation forces and average transverse momentum of partons. As a by-product, we also obtain Sivers and worm-gear-T transverse momentum dependent (TMD) distributions, which allows us to construct a tomographic picture of the proton based on substantially broader data.

Final states with several jets from the decays of heavy particles pose a combinatorial problem: the jets must be assigned, at least implicitly, to their parent particles. The Combinatorial Residual Network (CoReNet) is a classifier that encodes the assumed decay chain in its architecture, building the event representation level by level along the decay hierarchy and combining all jet assignment hypotheses, evaluated with shared weights, with learned weights. The exchange symmetries of the decay are built in, the network size does not depend on the number of hypotheses, and no generator-level jet assignments are used in training. Developed for the $b\bar{b}b\bar{b}$ final state and used in several CMS searches, CoReNet with 1508 parameters performs well above kinematic baselines on fast-simulated Higgs boson pair production against QCD multijet events and trains in minutes on a single GPU, and its hypothesis weights select the truth-matched jet pairing in most signal events in which it is defined. Since only the encoded decay chain is specific to the final state, we test the construction on $HH \to b\bar{b}W^+W^-$ against semileptonic $t\bar{t}$, where encoding the decay chain of the background as well improves the classification at a cost of about $10^{3}$ parameters. In both final states, CoReNet performs comparably to a state-of-the-art transformer-based network more than two orders of magnitude larger. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/cms-cmu/CoReNet.

♻ ☆ Symmetry-based resolution of pseudogauge ambiguities in local equilibrium
Carlos Hoyos
The total angular momentum current can be decomposed into orbital and spin contributions in different ways, known as pseudogauges. This freedom leads to ambiguities in the definition of local-equilibrium density operators, which in turn affect estimates of spin polarization in heavy-ion collisions. In this work, the pseudogauge ambiguity, together with other ambiguities associated with improvements of conserved currents, is reformulated in terms of spurious symmetries corresponding to conserved currents with vanishing total charge. A prescription for the unambiguous definition of a local-equilibrium density operator, defined as deviating from global equilibrium only by small gradients, is introduced using the currents associated with genuine symmetries. The resulting density operator is invariant under transformations that add improvement terms to local currents, including the energy-momentum tensor.

We focus in particular on two-point correlation functions at large angular scales, where signatures of nontrivial spatial topology may survive as relics of primordial physics. We investigate the observational consequences of toroidal compactification and analyze their impact on the primordial power spectrum of the CMB provided by the Planck satellite. Within the current experimental and theoretical uncertainties, we identify a possible indication closely related to spatial-parity breaking, consistent with the presence of six spatial extra dimensions in the early Universe, compactified at the GUT epoch before the start of inflation. Finally, we extend our framework to B-mode polarization, highlighting its potential as a sensitive probe in forthcoming ground-based and space-borne experiments with unprecedented precision.

Two statements follow from the analytic expressions. The $d$-quark contributions to $E_T$ and $\tilde{H}_T$ are equal and opposite in the chiral limit, the breaking being proportional to the quark mass and to the twist-six amplitude $\mathcal{V}_6$. At the level of the least suppressed momentum-fraction integral, the isoscalar tensor charge receives no leading-twist contribution, the twist-three terms of the two flavours cancelling. The LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment recently reported a single event consistent with a nuclear recoil of $E_{\rm NR}\sim248$~keV in an extended-energy search. We study the accompanying inelastic-xenon channel, $χ+Xe\toχ+Xe^{*}$, as a complementary test of dark matter (DM) interpretations of such high-recoil events. Using the non-relativistic effective-field-theory (NREFT) framework, we compute the inelastic-xenon rates for representative scenarios including accelerated DM populations and inelastic dark matter. Their signal patterns in the S1--S2 plane are reconstructed. The nuclear de-excitation shifts these signals toward the electronic-recoil band, where they may overlap with clustered isotope backgrounds. We then propose a schematic, physics-motivated background model to estimate their detectability. For many benchmarks, the inelastic-xenon rates are $\mathcal{O}(0.1)$ of the elastic rates or below, and the projected sensitivity remains weak even at $200~{\rm tonne\,yr}$ for the scenarios investigated. Our results provide additional inelastic-xenon signal predictions for various DM scenarios and motivate improved high-energy background modeling and detector calibration for future searches.

We propose a novel muon Moonshot concept for lunar subsurface tomography based on upward-going muons originating from the lunar regolith. Unlike Earth, the Moon lacks an atmosphere, leaving dense regolith below and a near-vacuum environment above. Consequently, most downward-going hadrons are absorbed before decaying, while upward-going hadrons escaping the regolith can decay in flight, producing a significant flux of lunar muons. These muons can be detected by instruments on the lunar surface or in near-lunar orbit. We perform Monte Carlo simulations to investigate their energy spectra, angular distributions, and integrated fluxes under various theoretical and detector configurations. The results indicate that the lunar muon flux is sensitive to detector altitude under idealized geometry. This dependence demonstrates its potential as a novel, non-invasive probe of shallow subsurface voids. We also present case studies on the detection of underground cavities and water resources. For shallow overburden, large cavity signals remain detectable with estimated backgrounds and systematics. Weaker water signals remain challenging. Potential implementations in future lunar missions are also discussed.

Therefore, deviations of measurements from SM predictions can be indications of new physics. With recent advances in experimental and analysis techniques, measurements of $\sin^2θ^\ell_{\rm eff}$ at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), extracted from the forward-backward asymmetry ($A_{\rm FB}$) in Drell-Yan dilepton events, are now competitive with previously published measurements at $e^+e^-$ collider experiments. We obtain $\sin^2θ^\ell_{\rm eff}$=0.23154$\pm$0.00024 with additional PDF constraints from measurements of the W decay lepton charge asymmetry at 13 TeV and the W/Z cross section ratios. It is the most precise single experiment measurement to date and is in excellent agreement with the SM 2026 indirect prediction of 0.23152$\pm$0.00006.

♻ ☆ Weyl conformal geometry vs Riemannian geometry of Weyl gauge invariant (dressed) metric

Weyl conformal geometry is the natural underlying geometry of gauge theories of Weyl group (of dilatations and Poincaré symmetry), such as Weyl quadratic gravity and its generalisation, Weyl-Dirac-Born-Infeld action (WDBI). These are local, Weyl-anomaly free (quantum) gauge theories of gravity. We describe Weyl gauge symmetry from a more familiar Riemannian view of Weyl gauge invariant dressed fields by the Wilson line of dilatations. Weyl geometry can then be seen as Riemannian geometry of non-local dressed metric ($g_{μν}^*$), at the "cost" of (gauge-induced) non-commutativity in the UV, due to Wilson line. Then Weyl quadratic gravity and WDBI actions of Weyl geometry, which are Weyl gauge invariant in $d$ dimensions, have the same expression in Riemannian geometry defined by $g^*_{μν}$. This is a non-local map and dual description of the two geometries and actions in the symmetric phase. Unlike for the metric, the equation of motion of Weyl gauge field ($ω_μ$) does not commute with the dressing of the metric. Quantum non-locality, in particular entanglement, and non-commutativity are (gauge-invariant) physical artefacts of "translating" (local) Weyl geometry and Weyl gauge covariance into our real-world Riemannian geometry of Weyl gauge invariant observables, and they are evidence of Weyl gauge symmetry. At lower energies, $ω_μ$ becomes massive, can decouple and Einstein-Hilbert action and commutativity are recovered. The case of a light $ω_μ$ is also discussed.

Because some modes feature temporarily tachyonic masses, they can be efficiently produced, and a significant fraction of the energy density released in the phase transition can get converted to particles rather than gradient energy. In this work, we introduce the SUrrogate ReFerence (SURF) method, a new approach to validating generative models. This framework enables exact Neyman-Pearson tests by training the target model on samples from another tractable surrogate, which is itself trained on real data. We argue that the EPiC-FM generative model is a valid surrogate reference for JetClass jets and apply SURF to show that modern jet taggers may already be operating close to the true statistical limit. We study a surprisingly efficient family of variational ansatze for the ground state of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics at large $N$. These are ansatze whose norm-squared probability distributions are themselves matrix integrals with single-trace actions, and so have their own independent `t Hooft expansions. They are efficient in the sense that optimizing over a small number of parameters produces many digits of accuracy for the energy, single-trace moments, and connected correlators. For infinite-$N$ planar data our results rapidly converge to within published bootstrap intervals and stabilize to a few digits of precision beyond them. We also demonstrate that we can efficiently capture $1/N$ corrections by computing connected two-point functions. These are matched against resummed quantum perturbation theory and Monte Carlo simulations.

At $λ_\pm$, the stabilizer is simple of type $E_6$, and the corresponding cubic is linearly equivalent to the complex Albert algebra cubic norm. The two cubics at $λ_\pm$, which we call critical, define complex-conjugate $E_6$-reductions of the complexified bundle. At any element with nonzero critical norm, the corresponding cubic determines a complex Albert algebra with basepoint stabilizer $F_4$; a line subbundle of the tangent bundle selects a smooth bundle of these algebras with tensorial operations and a Euclidean real form. The induced Levi-Civita connection preserves either critical cubic exactly when the $G_2$-structure is torsion-free. Geometry enters quantum theory in two places. The space of quantum states carries a symplectic form, which generates unitary evolution, and a metric, which governs uncertainties and transition probabilities. The classical phase space acquires a metric of its own when a vacuum is chosen: quantizing a linear system amounts to choosing a compatible complex structure, equivalently a compatible metric $g$. We take this second metric as the primary object and show that it plays, on phase space, the role that the quantum metric plays on the space of states: fluctuations of linear observables are $g$-norms of Hamiltonian vector fields, and along coherent states $g/2\hbar$ \emph{is} the quantum metric. Squeezed states then have a simple description. A squeezed vacuum is the vacuum of another metric, and squeezing is a property of a pair of metrics, a relative vacuum, whose invariants are the eigenvalues $e^{\pm2r_i}$ of $L=g_0^{-1}g$. We work out the harmonic oscillator in detail, including why a rotated squeezed state no longer minimizes the product of the displayed uncertainties. Quadratic evolution deforms the metric, and only the part of the generator that is self-adjoint with respect to the reference changes the $r_i$, at a rate we give exactly. For fields, a vacuum is unitarily implementable relative to a reference exactly when it lies at finite distance from it in the space of vacua. For a massless field in de Sitter space we revisit the two canonical charts compared by Grain and Vennin: relative to the reference of the standard squeezing formalism the Bunch--Davies state has $\sinh r_k=1/(2|kη|)$, and relative to the vacuum that a radiation era beginning at time $η$ would select it has $\sinh r_k=1/(2k^2η^2)$. The second comparison squeezes twice as fast and is unitarily implementable; the first is not.

Instant Folded Strings (IFSs) present a puzzle. On the one hand, they appear to be an intrinsic part of string theory: they are fundamental closed strings nucleated classically in backgrounds in which the string coupling grows toward the future, and they have been argued to play an important role in black-hole interiors and cosmology. On the other hand, their energy-momentum tensor violates the Averaged Null Energy Condition (ANEC), placing IFSs in tension with standard causality and unitarity arguments. We show that finite string coupling resolves this tension by triggering a decay cascade that saturates the ANEC in Minkowski spacetime. The remnant of the original IFS persists indefinitely, continuously seeding a self-similar fragmentation cascade that produces infinitely many strings over its full history. In the semiclassical regime, the cascade is governed by a single Malthusian exponent, $κ_{\mathrm{IFS}}=2\sqrt{2}-2$, which controls the branching growth, pressure decay, cutoff-ANEC convergence, and anomalous non-integer dependence on the string coupling. The complete state has vanishing total energy and momentum while remaining highly excited and carrying negative integrated pressure on every finite time slice. This provides a concrete example of genuinely stringy low-energy dynamics in which microscopic null-energy consistency coexists with macroscopic negative pressure.

We illustrate it on a Weyl BMS-type solution space with time-dependent boundary metric, described in tetrad variables with a residual U(1) Lorentz freedom, for which the cocycle of a naive lift is computed and then explicitly removed.

These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly. The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students. The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material. Developments after spring 2025 are not covered, but the basic ideas emphasized here are unlikely to go out of date soon.

In this paper, we introduce and validate a new method to solve this moment problem using the maximum entropy principle. The method reconstructs, at each order of truncation, the least-biased transmission probability compatible with a finite set of KdV integrals, guaranteeing positivity by construction. We first validate the technique against the exactly solvable Pöschl-Teller potential. We then apply it to the Regge-Wheeler potential governing axial perturbations of a Schwarzschild BH, where no exact solution is available; the resulting reconstruction agrees closely with the fourth-order Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin (WKB) approximation across several multipoles. This is the first application of the maximum entropy method to the reconstruction of BH greybody factors, demonstrating that a modest number of KdV integrals is sufficient to recover them accurately.

The bound holds for each fixed pair of distinct Majorana modes in the SYK model and for the target average of any fixed single-site source in the spin model. At vanishing external spatial momentum, for pairs built from QNM branches with opposite real parts, the leading light-cone contributions cancel at large momentum, and the residual QNM-pair frequency scales as $q^{-1/3}$. Consequently, an infinite family of cuts accumulates at zero frequency, while all tree-level QNM poles remain at finite nonzero frequencies. The first finite-$N$ correction therefore closes the gap set by the classical QNM spectrum. Competition between the decreasing QNM-pair damping and thermal Boltzmann suppression produces a moving saddle and a finite-$N$ contribution $G(t)\sim N^{-2}t^αe^{-Ct^{3/4}},\, C>0,$ which decays more slowly than the leading classical QNM contribution. Thus the large-$N$ expansion is nonuniform at late times, and bulk quantum fluctuations generate a distinct late-time regime beyond the classical QNM decay.

We also give a continuum interpretation of these results in terms of inflow from a gravitational Chern Simons theory which is induced by integrating out massive bulk Kähler Dirac fermions. In the presence of a boundary the latter gives rise to Wen-Zee terms that mediate the anomaly inflow mechanism.

An upshot of our finding is that quantum field theories formulated relative to a quantum reference frame cannot rest on the traditional axioms, and some general relational axiomatisation must replace at least some of them by taking into account physically realistic properties of the frame.

Generic lightlike solutions preserve four real supercharges, whereas spacelike and timelike solutions preserve eight, with a Killing superalgebra containing a single exceptional $\mathfrak d(2,1;α)$ factor.

☆ Gravity/Thermodynamics Correspondence for Generic Dynamical Spacetimes

Working within covariant phase space formalism, we establish \textit{gravity-thermodynamics correspondence} for generic dynamical spacetimes. We derive local first and second laws of thermodynamics on general null boundaries, for generic non-stationary solutions to Einstein gravity {with minimally coupled matter} for physical observers that we carefully specify. Entropy variation, which receives contribution only from the gravitational sector, is the surface charge variation associated with a vector field generating the null boundary, and temperature is its non-affinity parameter (divided by $2π$). The statement of the second law in our setting is that the entropy variation evaluated along the null vector field is strictly non-negative for the admissible positive-non-affinity clock and matter satisfying the null energy condition. Our dynamical entropy variation, which is non-integrable for generic non-stationary solutions, becomes integrable in near-stationary configurations, reproducing the Hollands--Wald--Zhang dynamical entropy formula. Strikingly, this local second law holds even when the boundary area is decreasing, disentangling thermodynamic irreversibility and the second law from standard area theorems. Our first-principles construction demonstrates that gravitational thermodynamics requires neither a stationary background, teleological event horizons, nor an exact entropy state function on individual codimension-1 spacelike slices of the null boundary (codimension two in spacetime).

Since there is no known nonperturbative instability in this DGKT vacuum, this provides evidence that the IIA SUSY-broken AdS vacua may be absolutely stable. We also find the weak fake superpotential exists locally in field space in some SUSY-broken AdS vacua in a KKLT construction in IIB. Thus, within the framework considered here, some false SUSY-broken KKLT AdS vacua are stable against vacuum decay. Conversely, we find that some KKLT vacua do not have a weak fake superpotential, and correspondingly violate the Penrose Inequality and fail to have a positive mass theorem; the DGKT vacua only violate the Penrose Inequality in the presence of designer gravity boundary conditions. In all cases studied, this is due to false vacuum decay. We discuss the implications of these violations for holography and black hole thermodynamics in these SUSY-broken AdS vacua.

We also discuss Oshikawa's flux insertion arguments for FL, and their extension to FL*, including a discussion of gapless spin liquids.
